c.tagline: Where Brazil began — the Discovery Coast's colonial cliff-top and endless Bahia beaches.

taxi.fareNote: City taxis are metered; agree a flat rate for longer resort or beach runs, and expect surcharges at night.

emergency.note: 190 reaches the military police, 192 the SAMU ambulance service, and 193 the fire brigade.

hood_landmark.Arraial d'Ajuda: Arraial d'Ajuda church cliff Porto Seguro

avoid.reason: Avoid the peripheral Baianão complex and other outlying favela districts, where most of the city's violent crime is concentrated.
Watch for pickpockets along the Passarela do Álcool and beach clubs, and avoid deserted stretches of beach after dark.

hood_desc: The Cidade Histórica perched on a high bluff over the ocean — a living museum of 16th-century colonial churches, the old jailhouse and grassy squares where Brazil's story began; best for history and sunset views.
The lively downtown seafront around the Passarela do Álcool, a nightly open-air strip of bars, craft stalls, capirinha vendors and street music; best for nightlife and dining.
Porto Seguro's prime beach strip north of town, lined with beach clubs, big resorts and calm reef-protected water; best for beach days and family resorts.
The northern coastal sprawl toward Coroa Vermelha, with reef pools, an indigenous craft market and the cross marking Brazil's first Mass; a quieter, spread-out resort area.
A bohemian beach village across the Buranhém River ferry, with a cliff-top church, Mucugê beach and the Broadway bar-and-restaurant strip; a laid-back but lively alternative base.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water; tap water is not reliably potable.

transit.hours: Municipal buses run roughly 5:30 AM to 11:00 PM; late-night trips rely on taxis and ride apps.
transit.note: Porto Seguro has no metro or rail; municipal buses, taxis, ride-hailing apps and the passenger/car ferry across the Buranhém River to Arraial d'Ajuda are the main ways to get around.
transit.pay: Bus fares are paid in cash to the onboard conductor; there is no rechargeable transit-card system.

bus: Intercity coaches to Salvador, Eunápolis and Vitória (Rodoviária de Porto Seguro)
ferry: Buranhém River car & passenger ferry to Arraial d'Ajuda

tip.r: A 10% service charge is usually added to restaurant bills; extra tipping is appreciated but not expected.

food.desc: Fish or prawns stewed in a clay pot with coconut milk, dende palm oil, peppers and coriander, served bubbling with rice, farofa and pirao.

places.name: Colher de Pau
places.note: Award-winning local restaurant whose moquecas and lobster are the reason regulars keep coming back.

places.name: Vovo Bela

places.name: Casarao Adega Resto

food.name: Acaraje
food.desc: Black-eyed pea fritter deep-fried in dende, split and stuffed with vatapa, caruru, dried shrimp and hot pepper sauce - Bahia's iconic street food.

places.name: Acaraje da Jaque
places.note: Much-recommended stall serving acaraje with the full set of vatapa, caruru, shrimp and tomato.

places.name: Acaraje Gourmet

places.name: Centro Historico evening vendors

food.name: Casquinha de Siri
food.desc: Picked crab meat cooked with coconut milk, dende and herbs, packed back into a shell and gratinated with farofa - the classic Bahian beach starter.

places.name: Taperapuan beach barracas
places.note: The big beach clubs along Taperapuan serve casquinha with cold beer all afternoon.

places.name: Colher de Pau
places.note: Long-established kitchen that does the traditional seafood starters properly.

places.name: Vovo Bela
places.note: Dependable spot for crab, prawn and fish starters before a moqueca.

food.name: Bobo de Camarao
food.desc: Prawns simmered in a thick puree of cassava, coconut milk and dende - richer and smoother than moqueca, eaten with white rice.

places.name: Casarao Adega Resto
places.note: Contemporary takes on Bahian seafood classics in an elegant promenade setting.

places.name: Colher de Pau
places.note: Award-listed restaurant covering the full Bahian repertoire of prawn and cassava dishes.

food.desc: Cassava-starch crepes cooked dry on a hot plate and folded around coconut, cheese or condensed milk - a Pataxo staple turned beach snack.

places.name: Acaraje Gourmet

places.name: Taperapuan beach barracas

food.name: Cocada
food.desc: Shredded coconut boiled with sugar into chewy white or dark-caramel squares, sold in stacks by beach vendors up and down the Bahian coast.

places.name: Passarela do Alcool sweet stalls
places.note: Trays of white and burnt cocada sold nightly along the main tourist strip.

places.name: Taperapuan beach vendors
places.note: Vendors work the sand all day with cocada, cashew brittle and coconut sweets.

places.name: Centro Historico craft stalls
places.note: Old-town stalls sell homemade cocada and other Bahian sweets beside the handicrafts.

food.name: Capeta
food.desc: Porto Seguro's own cocktail - vodka shaken with condensed milk, guarana powder, cinnamon and ice into a sweet, caffeinated nightcap.

places.note: The strip where capeta was popularised; dozens of carts mix it to order after dark.

places.name: Acaraje Gourmet

places.name: Taperapuan beach clubs

food.name: Agua de Coco
food.desc: Green coconut water drunk straight from the nut with a straw, then split open so you can scrape out the soft jelly inside.

places.name: Taperapuan beach barracas

landmarks: Centro Historico (Cidade Alta)
Perched above the sea where Brazil began in 1500, whitewashed churches and the Marco do Descobrimento landmark stone recall the Portuguese arrival.
Igreja de Nossa Senhora da Pena
The 18th-century landmark church of the upper town shelters a revered image of St. Francis considered among the oldest sacred artworks in Brazil.
Passarela do Descobrimento (Passarela do Alcool)
By night this seafront promenade of brightly painted colonial houses becomes a carnival of capeta cocktail stalls, craft vendors and street musicians.
Memorial da Epopeia do Descobrimento
A full-scale replica Portuguese nau anchors this waterfront museum-garden narrating the 1500 landfall and the Tupi world that met the caravels.
Praia de Taperapua
Porto Seguro's most famous beach pulses with axe music at mega beach clubs like Axe Moi and Toa Toa between swims in warm shallows.
Reserva da Jaqueira
The Pataxo community welcomes visitors to this forest reserve for body painting, archery and a moving introduction to indigenous Bahian culture.
Arraial d'Ajuda
Across the Buranhem River by quick ferry, this bohemian clifftop village charms with Mucuge street boutiques, a pretty church square and gorgeous Pitinga beach.
Marco do Descobrimento
A stone monument in the historic center marking the spot where Portuguese explorers first claimed Brazil in 1500, carved with a cross and royal coat of arms.
Farol de Porto Seguro
A white lighthouse standing since 1907 atop the hill where the city was founded, giving one of the best views over the coast.
Museu de Porto Seguro
A small history museum in the historic center's old council house, tracing the town's role as the birthplace of colonial Brazil.

train.note: No railway serves Porto Seguro, and Brazil has no intercity passenger trains. Arrive by coach on the BR-367, by car, or on one of the frequent flights from São Paulo and Rio.

bus.note: No international coaches. The Rodoviária is a few kilometres from the historic centre, with Águia Branca and Gontijo services to Salvador (about 11 hours), Vitória and Belo Horizonte; book through ClickBus (https://www.clickbus.com.br/). Local buses and vans run down to Trancoso and Caraíva once you have crossed the river.

intl.to: Arraial d'Ajuda (Brazil) - ~10 min across the Rio Buranhém, 24 hr
intl.op: Balsa Porto Seguro-Arraial d'Ajuda — tickets at the ramp

ferry.note: There are no international sailings. The little car-and-passenger balsa across the Buranhém river runs continuously day and night and is the only practical way to reach Arraial d'Ajuda, Trancoso and Caraíva - the road route is a long detour inland. Crossings take about ten minutes; vehicle queues build up badly over New Year and Carnival.

full.blurb: Chic beach town around the grassy Quadrado square, with a whitewashed church, boutiques and upscale restaurants.
